claims.text: The initial equiatomic Au-Co-Cu-Ni-Pt nanoparticles have a disordered solid-solution structure.
The sluggish-diffusion assumption breaks down for Au-Co-Cu-Ni-Pt nanoparticles smaller than 5 nm.
A high surface-to-volume ratio causes surface diffusion to dominate structural evolution.
Curvature-driven mass transport becomes dominant in the sub-5 nm regime.
Surface-energy minimization drives rapid Ostwald ripening during vacuum heating.
The nanoparticles undergo spinodal-like surface segregation during heating.
The driving force for reducing total surface energy overcomes the kinetic barrier to atomic diffusion.
Surface-energy-driven evolution negates high-entropy stabilization in particles below the critical size.
Particles smaller than 5 nm rapidly disappear during heating to 1000 K.
Larger particles grow as the smallest particles disappear.
The particle surface becomes enriched in the constituent having the lowest surface energy.
Au is likely the constituent toward which the surface composition shifts.
Heating changes particle morphology from spherical to faceted or irregular shapes.
For particles larger than 10 nm, sluggish diffusion may remain the dominant mechanism.
Prior theory predicts that high-entropy effects and sluggish diffusion preserve the equiatomic disordered structure and particle-size distribution up to 1000 K.
The exact critical size for the transition to surface-energy-driven behavior is unknown.
Experimental data are lacking for this quinary system under the specified heating conditions.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis and boundary specify a critical cutoff of less than 5 nm, while the uncertainty field states that the exact critical size is unknown. The 5–10 nm interval is also left without a clear regime assignment.
